evidence_claims.title: Soft Robotic Grippers Based on Particle Transmission
evidence_claims.claim: Using particle transmission driven by a motor-actuated piston circumvents fluid-sealing challenges while enabling combined actuation and variable stiffness without bulky pumps or valve manifolds.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Robotic Grippers Based on Particle Transmission
evidence_claims.claim: Injecting solid particles up to 1.8 times the initial volume produces bending up to 60 degrees and increases rotational stiffness by nearly seven-fold from the unactuated state.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Robotic Grippers Based on Particle Transmission
evidence_claims.claim: Kinematic bending range and rotational stiffness can be modeled analytically by assuming torus segment expansion and calculating inter-particle contact forces and friction moments from Neo-Hookean membrane tension.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Robotic Grippers Based on Particle Transmission
evidence_claims.claim: Solid glassy glass balls demonstrated superior performance over stainless steel balls, plastic balls, and beans owing to high hardness, low thermal conductivity, and small friction coefficient.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Robotic Grippers Based on Particle Transmission
evidence_claims.claim: Smaller particle diameters (2 mm vs. 3 mm and 4 mm) generate a more linear bending response, larger angular deflection, and higher rotational stiffness.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Robotic Grippers Based on Particle Transmission
evidence_claims.claim: At an injected volume ratio of 1.8, particle transmission generates nearly six-fold greater stiffness and over five-fold greater bending deflection than compressed air, and roughly three-fold higher stiffness than water.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Robotic Grippers Based on Particle Transmission
evidence_claims.claim: Incomplete elastic restoration occurs after piston retraction due to inter-particle jamming, but embedding miniature vibrators into the strain-limiting layer enables complete recovery to the initial position.

evidence_claims.title: Novel Variable-Stiffness Robotic Fingers with Built-In Position Feedback
evidence_claims.claim: Soft robotic fingers achieve variable stiffness by modulating shape memory polymer (SMP) temperature around its glass transition temperature using embedded conductive TPU heaters, exhibiting an 8.18-fold stiffness change at zero air pressure.

evidence_claims.title: Novel Variable-Stiffness Robotic Fingers with Built-In Position Feedback
evidence_claims.claim: Conductive TPU elastomer performs dual roles within a soft finger joint as an embedded Joule heating element and a piezoresistive strain sensor for position estimation.

evidence_claims.title: Novel Variable-Stiffness Robotic Fingers with Built-In Position Feedback
evidence_claims.claim: Concurrent fused deposition modeling (FDM) 3D printing produces an interlocking multi-material substrate of SMP and conductive TPU in a single setup without assembly.

evidence_claims.title: Novel Variable-Stiffness Robotic Fingers with Built-In Position Feedback
evidence_claims.claim: A theoretical model relating primary shape volume/cross-section changes of conductive TPU to carbon black volume fraction predicts electrical resistance variation consistent with experimental results up to 90 degrees of joint bending.

evidence_claims.title: Novel Variable-Stiffness Robotic Fingers with Built-In Position Feedback
evidence_claims.claim: Preheating conductive TPU/SMP joints to 35 °C reduces thermal activation time from room temperature (40 s) to under 10 s with 0.75 W power input.

evidence_claims.title: Novel Variable-Stiffness Robotic Fingers with Built-In Position Feedback
evidence_claims.claim: Passive convective ventilation features integrated into the finger substrate accelerate cooling, reducing cooling duration from 50 °C to 45 °C from 30 s to 15 s when increasing ventilation area.

evidence_claims.title: Novel Variable-Stiffness Robotic Fingers with Built-In Position Feedback
evidence_claims.claim: Increasing pneumatic actuator air pressure increases overall baseline finger stiffness and reduces the relative stiffness modulation ratio achieved by thermal SMP modulus changes.

evidence_claims.title: Novel Variable-Stiffness Robotic Fingers with Built-In Position Feedback
evidence_claims.claim: Optical tracking of fingertip reference point coordinates closely matches kinematic predictions derived from conductive TPU joint resistance measurements across pneumatic pressures from 0 to 100 kPa.

evidence_claims.title: Shape Memory Alloy-Based Soft Gripper with Variable Stiffness for Compliant and Effective Grasping
evidence_claims.claim: Embedding 3D-printed shape memory polymer (SMP) structures inside soft composite hinges enables an approximate 55-fold reversible change in bending modulus between glassy and rubbery states (128.48 MPa vs. 2.31 MPa).

evidence_claims.title: Shape Memory Alloy-Based Soft Gripper with Variable Stiffness for Compliant and Effective Grasping
evidence_claims.claim: Actuation of symmetrically placed off-center SMA wires combined with selective heating of two independent SMP hinges enables a single soft robotic finger to achieve nine distinct active configurations and retain them with high stiffness.

evidence_claims.title: Shape Memory Alloy-Based Soft Gripper with Variable Stiffness for Compliant and Effective Grasping
evidence_claims.claim: Modulating hinge stiffness from low to high after conforming to an object increases the soft gripper's maximum vertical pulling force by approximately 10 times (from 0.6 N to 5.8 N).

evidence_claims.title: Shape Memory Alloy-Based Soft Gripper with Variable Stiffness for Compliant and Effective Grasping
evidence_claims.claim: The bending modulus of the composite variable-stiffness hinge can be theoretically predicted using second moment of area formulations and constituent elastic moduli, showing agreement within 5.6% and 1.7% of experimental values.

evidence_claims.title: Shape Memory Alloy-Based Soft Gripper with Variable Stiffness for Compliant and Effective Grasping
evidence_claims.claim: Integrating a soft Ecoflex layer at the fingertip pad increases compliant contact area and moment resistance, preventing slippage and allowing stable grasping of difficult frustum-shaped geometries compared to rigid point contacts.

evidence_claims.title: Shape Memory Alloy-Based Soft Gripper with Variable Stiffness for Compliant and Effective Grasping
evidence_claims.claim: Heating the SMP to rubbery state requires approximately 35 seconds, whereas passive cooling back to the glassy state requires approximately 240 seconds, representing the primary operational time bottleneck.

evidence_claims.title: A Soft Robotic Gripper With Gecko-Inspired Adhesive
evidence_claims.claim: Integrating directional gecko-inspired adhesives onto fluidic elastomer actuators decouples grasp strength from high normal force and high internal fluid pressure by leveraging adhesion-controlled friction.

evidence_claims.title: A Soft Robotic Gripper With Gecko-Inspired Adhesive
evidence_claims.claim: Fluidic elastomer actuators can be modeled as a series of discrete joints where joint torque depends on internal pressure, membrane area, and neutral axis distance, enabling actuators to follow a modified Hirose torque distribution that maintains surface contact area under pressurization.

evidence_claims.title: A Soft Robotic Gripper With Gecko-Inspired Adhesive
evidence_claims.claim: Using Frustrated Total Internal Reflection (FTIR), an actuator designed with a Hirose torque distribution maintained high contact area across increasing pressures, whereas an actuator with a uniform torque profile lost contact as distal joints overpowered proximal joints.

evidence_claims.title: A Soft Robotic Gripper With Gecko-Inspired Adhesive
evidence_claims.claim: In cylinder pullout tests at 27 kPa, the gecko elastomer actuator gripper produced 35.7 N higher grasp force on a 57 mm cylinder (348% increase) and 8.58 N higher force on a 203 mm cylinder (2095% increase) compared to an identical non-adhesive elastomer gripper.

evidence_claims.title: A Soft Robotic Gripper With Gecko-Inspired Adhesive
evidence_claims.claim: On dusty, rocky, or irregular objects where adhesive performance is diminished, the gecko elastomer actuator gripper maintains baseline force-closure functionality with no measured loss in performance relative to conventional elastomer grippers.

evidence_claims.title: A Soft Robotic Gripper With Gecko-Inspired Adhesive
evidence_claims.claim: A three-finger gecko elastomer gripper mounted on a KUKA LBR iiwa robot arm supported and manipulated an 11.3 kg (111 N / 25 lbf) payload at 40 kPa internal pressure across more than 25 trials without visible damage or performance loss.

evidence_claims.title: A Soft Robotic Gripper With Gecko-Inspired Adhesive
evidence_claims.claim: Directional gecko adhesives require shear loading to engage; on curved surfaces shear is induced passively by object geometry, whereas flat surfaces lack passive shear and require high bending stiffness or actuation-independent stiffening mechanisms.

evidence_claims.title: A Variable Stiffness Robotic Gripper Based on Structure-Controlled Principle
evidence_claims.claim: Rotating an embedded flexure hinge shaft relative to a stationary flexure housing alters the effective second moment of area, modulating Cartesian stiffness continuously following a cosine curve as a function of the rotation angle.

evidence_claims.title: A Variable Stiffness Robotic Gripper Based on Structure-Controlled Principle
evidence_claims.claim: Adopting corner-filleted flexure hinges of short length instead of uniform leaf springs suppresses lateral buckling during rotation, as the critical buckling load increases inversely with the square of hinge length.

evidence_claims.title: A Variable Stiffness Robotic Gripper Based on Structure-Controlled Principle
evidence_claims.claim: Non-back-drivable worm gear transmission holds the rotation angle of the inner flexure shaft without requiring active motor torque or electrical power to maintain finger stiffness.

evidence_claims.title: A Variable Stiffness Robotic Gripper Based on Structure-Controlled Principle
evidence_claims.claim: Finite element analysis in ANSYS predicts a fatigue life of 1.8 x 10^4 cycles under zero-based bending at the lowest stiffness state, exceeding the 10^4 cycle design target.

evidence_claims.title: A Variable Stiffness Robotic Gripper Based on Structure-Controlled Principle
evidence_claims.claim: The prototype finger achieved an empirical stiffness range ratio of approximately 53.3, with measured stiffness varying between 0.13 N/mm and 4.99 N/mm over rotation angles from 0 to 63 degrees.

evidence_claims.title: A Variable Stiffness Robotic Gripper Based on Structure-Controlled Principle
evidence_claims.claim: Fast dynamic grasping at the highest stiffness state caused an instantaneous impact force overshoot of approximately 30%, whereas grasping at the lowest stiffness state exhibited a gradual rise to the target force without overshoot.

evidence_claims.title: A Variable Stiffness Robotic Gripper Based on Structure-Controlled Principle
evidence_claims.claim: At the lowest stiffness state (0.13 N/mm), the gripper passively accommodated position misalignments up to 17 mm with a contact force of approximately 2.2 N.

evidence_claims.title: A Variable Stiffness Robotic Gripper Based on Structure-Controlled Principle
evidence_claims.claim: The gripper successfully grasped eight varied objects spanning 5.0 g to 500 g (including an eggshell, raw egg, tomato, stone, and metal block) under open-loop position control without tactile/force sensors or soft rubber pads.

evidence_claims.title: Modeling of grasping force for a soft robotic gripper with variable stiffness
evidence_claims.claim: Structural decoupling of bending actuation and variable stiffness mechanisms is realized using separate shape memory alloy elements: an electrothermal contracting SMA-1 fiber for bending actuation, thermal-induced SMA-2 wires without length change for variable stiffness, and a superelastic SMA-3 central wire for elastic restoration.

evidence_claims.title: Modeling of grasping force for a soft robotic gripper with variable stiffness
evidence_claims.claim: The response characteristics of the soft finger backbone do not comply with constant-curvature models when subjected to combined gravity, grasping contact forces, and driving torques, necessitating a Cosserat rod theory formulation.

evidence_claims.title: Modeling of grasping force for a soft robotic gripper with variable stiffness
evidence_claims.claim: Increasing the Young's modulus of the SMA-2 variable stiffness wires from 25 GPa to 48 GPa via electrical heating increases the maximum grasping force of the soft finger by 48.7% experimentally and 42.5% in simulation.

evidence_claims.title: Modeling of grasping force for a soft robotic gripper with variable stiffness
evidence_claims.claim: Increasing the object offset distance H from 30 mm to 60 mm increases the required no-load bending torque to reach contact but decreases the attainable maximum grasping force.

evidence_claims.title: Modeling of grasping force for a soft robotic gripper with variable stiffness
evidence_claims.claim: Finite element modeling in ABAQUS showed close agreement with the Cosserat rod formulation, exhibiting grasping force differences between 0.005 N and 0.032 N across object offsets from 30 mm to 60 mm at a bending torque of 20 Nmm.

evidence_claims.title: Modeling of grasping force for a soft robotic gripper with variable stiffness
evidence_claims.claim: Discrepancies observed between initial multi-finger gripper simulations and experiments were demonstrated not to stem from force closure failure or internal pulley friction, but from surface wear on 3D-printed PLA fingertips that lowered the contact friction coefficient from 0.426 to 0.335.
evidence_claims.evidence_type: experimental hypothesis testing and error analysis

evidence_claims.title: Soft Robotic Grippers
evidence_claims.claim: Soft gripping technologies can be systematically categorized into three main operating mechanisms: actuation, controlled stiffness, and controlled adhesion, which can also be combined into hybrid systems.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Robotic Grippers
evidence_claims.claim: Material compliance and underactuation allow soft grippers to passively conform to varied object geometries, lowering control complexity via morphological computation.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Robotic Grippers
evidence_claims.claim: Fluidic elastomer actuators (FEAs) generate high blocked forces (e.g., 80 N at 300 kPa and 112 N at 200 kPa) and large bending angles, but are constrained by the mass and size of external compressors and fluidic channel impedance restricting response frequencies above 1 Hz.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Robotic Grippers
evidence_claims.claim: Dielectric elastomer actuators (DEAs) offer rapid response times under 200 microseconds and high strains, but produce low active stress and generally require high operating voltages on the order of kilovolts.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Robotic Grippers
evidence_claims.claim: Granular jamming enables rapid reversible stiffness changes up to 24 times via vacuum-induced depressurization of granule-filled membranes, producing caging forces without high normal compressive loads, but cannot envelop flat objects.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Robotic Grippers
evidence_claims.claim: Low-melting point alloys (LMPAs) embedded in soft matrices demonstrate relative stiffness changes ranging from 25 to over 9000 times through thermal phase changes between 47 °C and 62 °C, though cooling times typically exceed 60 seconds.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Robotic Grippers
evidence_claims.claim: Electrorheological (ER) and magnetorheological (MR) fluids transition to viscoelastic states within 10 milliseconds upon application of electric or magnetic fields, but their overall solidified stiffness is constrained by yield stresses up to 250 kPa.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Robotic Grippers
evidence_claims.claim: Controlled adhesion mechanisms such as electroadhesion and geckoadhesion produce high shear holding forces with minimal normal compressive forces, enabling high lifting ratios (reported up to 286.7 for geckoadhesion and 54.7 for electroadhesion), but require clean and dry surfaces.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Robotic Grippers
evidence_claims.claim: Integrating stretchable resistive, capacitive, optical waveguide, and magnetic Hall-effect sensors into compliant gripper structures facilitates proprioceptive finger curvature detection and exteroceptive object tactile characterization.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Actuators with Stiffness and Shape Modulation Using 3D-Printed Conductive Polylactic Acid Material
evidence_claims.claim: Conductive polylactic acid (CPLA) displays a 98.6% reduction in Young's modulus from 1 GPa at room temperature (25°C) to 13.6 MPa at 80°C, and fully recovers its stiffness upon cooling back to room temperature.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Actuators with Stiffness and Shape Modulation Using 3D-Printed Conductive Polylactic Acid Material
evidence_claims.claim: Differential scanning calorimetry indicates that CPLA has a glass transition temperature of 55°C, where its Young's modulus decreases to 60% of its room-temperature value, and exhibits melting peaks at 124.4°C and 154°C.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Actuators with Stiffness and Shape Modulation Using 3D-Printed Conductive Polylactic Acid Material
evidence_claims.claim: A lumped-parameter dynamic heat transfer model with linearized temperature-dependent resistivity accurately predicts the Joule heating and passive cooling dynamics of CPLA, with passive cooling from the glass transition temperature to room temperature requiring approximately 120 s for a 10 mm x 10 mm x 2 mm sample.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Actuators with Stiffness and Shape Modulation Using 3D-Printed Conductive Polylactic Acid Material
evidence_claims.claim: Finite element simulation integrating an electrical system, steady-state thermal analysis, and an Ogden hyperelastic structural model predicts actuator bending angles with discrepancies generally under 2 degrees compared to experimental measurements (with errors of ~4 and ~7 degrees occurring only at 18 psi for Hinges 2 and 3).

evidence_claims.title: Soft Actuators with Stiffness and Shape Modulation Using 3D-Printed Conductive Polylactic Acid Material
evidence_claims.claim: Localized Joule heating of selected CPLA virtual hinges allows selective bending at targeted segments while unheated segments remain rigid, enabling reconfigurable bending shapes under pneumatic pressure.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Actuators with Stiffness and Shape Modulation Using 3D-Printed Conductive Polylactic Acid Material
evidence_claims.claim: A two-finger soft gripper employing CPLA-embedded actuators can execute distinct grasping postures (scooping, pinching, and parallel grabbing) to hold objects of varied geometry and compliance.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Actuators with Stiffness and Shape Modulation Using 3D-Printed Conductive Polylactic Acid Material
evidence_claims.claim: An actuator can lock its shape by cooling the CPLA hinges to room temperature while pressurized, successfully carrying a payload of up to 800 g passively without pressure or electrical power input.

evidence_claims.title: Variable Stiffness Robotic Hand for Stable Grasp and Flexible Handling
evidence_claims.claim: Coupling an object with unknown stiffness to a robotic gripper can shift system poles into the right half-plane and induce grasp instability, which can be mitigated by introducing passive compliance into the actuation system.
evidence_claims.evidence_type: Theoretical modeling and root locus analysis

evidence_claims.title: Variable Stiffness Robotic Hand for Stable Grasp and Flexible Handling
evidence_claims.claim: The apparent stiffness of the robotic hand is analytically governed by the angle between the tendon and the spring-loaded rod, varying from the linear spring constant K when parallel up to theoretically infinite stiffness when perpendicular.

evidence_claims.title: Variable Stiffness Robotic Hand for Stable Grasp and Flexible Handling
evidence_claims.claim: Static force-displacement characterization demonstrates that tendon elongation for a given applied tensile force decreases monotonically as the rod angle theta increases from 5 to 55 degrees.

evidence_claims.title: Variable Stiffness Robotic Hand for Stable Grasp and Flexible Handling
evidence_claims.claim: Increasing finger stiffness via the variable stiffness mechanism improves trajectory tracking accuracy under sinusoidal inputs and reduces the peak magnitude in frequency response Bode plots.
evidence_claims.evidence_type: Dynamic trajectory tracking and frequency analysis experiments

evidence_claims.title: Variable Stiffness Robotic Hand for Stable Grasp and Flexible Handling
evidence_claims.claim: The robotic hand exhibits mechanical hysteresis during cyclic tendon loading and unloading, but the hysteresis band narrows as the rod angle theta increases.

evidence_claims.title: Variable Stiffness Robotic Hand for Stable Grasp and Flexible Handling
evidence_claims.claim: A first-order sliding mode controller combined with an inner anti-windup PI velocity loop converges error states to zero in finite time and achieves stable grip force tracking across objects of varying stiffness with small steady-state error and zero or negligible overshoot.
evidence_claims.evidence_type: Robotic control experiment on hardware testbed

evidence_claims.title: Flexible Fingers Based on Shape Memory Alloy Actuated Modules
evidence_claims.claim: Modular flexible fingers actuated by three longitudinal SMA wires positioned at 120 degrees can achieve planar bending in any direction across 360 degrees, but inactive antagonistic SMA wires impose a major physical limitation on bending deformation.

evidence_claims.title: Flexible Fingers Based on Shape Memory Alloy Actuated Modules
evidence_claims.claim: A 2D static moment equilibrium model demonstrates that antagonist moments from inactive wires nearly balance the active SMA moment (e.g., 0.0400 Nm antagonist vs 0.0424 Nm SMA in main directions, and 0.0440 Nm antagonist vs 0.0454 Nm SMA in secondary directions), substantially restricting the resultant bending angle.

evidence_claims.title: Flexible Fingers Based on Shape Memory Alloy Actuated Modules
evidence_claims.claim: Experimental tests on prototypes with inactive antagonist wires physically disassembled demonstrated a significant increase in the reachable 3D workspace and planar displacement compared to configurations with antagonist wires present.

evidence_claims.title: Flexible Fingers Based on Shape Memory Alloy Actuated Modules
evidence_claims.claim: An SMA wire-driven locking and unlocking gripper-cylinder mechanism integrated into the module base releases inactive antagonist wires to slide freely during actuation, expanding the workspace compared to permanently locked antagonist configurations.

evidence_claims.title: Flexible Fingers Based on Shape Memory Alloy Actuated Modules
evidence_claims.claim: Material trade-offs govern module performance: nylon offers good flexibility but melts near SMA operating temperatures (~120 °C); PTFE resists temperature (250 °C) but exhibits reduced workspace due to pretension; silicone rubber (LIM) withstands high temperatures but lacks sufficient elastic recall force to return the module to its undeformed state.

evidence_claims.title: Long Shape Memory Alloy Tendon-based Soft Robotic Actuators and Implementation as a Soft Gripper
evidence_claims.claim: Decoupling the length of the polymeric matrix from the SMA wire by using free-sliding tendons through silicone tubes enables large increases in bending angle (up to 400 degrees) and tip force (up to 0.89 N).

evidence_claims.title: Long Shape Memory Alloy Tendon-based Soft Robotic Actuators and Implementation as a Soft Gripper
evidence_claims.claim: A quasi-static mechanical model coupling beam strain mechanics with Brinson's 1D SMA constitutive model accurately predicts bending angle as a function of tendon length up to physical contact limits.

evidence_claims.title: Long Shape Memory Alloy Tendon-based Soft Robotic Actuators and Implementation as a Soft Gripper
evidence_claims.claim: Uneven tendon lengths on either side of the U-shaped routing produce pure planar bending without torsion due to tension distribution through free sliding in the silicone sleeve.

evidence_claims.title: Long Shape Memory Alloy Tendon-based Soft Robotic Actuators and Implementation as a Soft Gripper
evidence_claims.claim: Modular finger packaging with V-shaped bearings routes 300 mm tendons compactly and withstands 100 continuous thermal cycles without degradation of maximum bending angle.

evidence_claims.title: Long Shape Memory Alloy Tendon-based Soft Robotic Actuators and Implementation as a Soft Gripper
evidence_claims.claim: Three-fingered antagonistic and triangular soft grippers adaptively grasp diverse objects weighing from 5 g up to 1.5 kg (and withstand a 2 kg test weight).

evidence_claims.title: Long Shape Memory Alloy Tendon-based Soft Robotic Actuators and Implementation as a Soft Gripper
evidence_claims.claim: The soft gripper achieves maximum pulling forces of 25 N in point contact and 30 N in power grasp using 0.305 mm SMA wires, maintaining high force over 40 mm displacement.

evidence_claims.title: Long Shape Memory Alloy Tendon-based Soft Robotic Actuators and Implementation as a Soft Gripper
evidence_claims.claim: Wrapping actuator fingers in a low-friction TPU-coated sleeve drops maximum pulling force from 25-30 N to 7-13 N, demonstrating the critical role of interfacial friction in load capacity.

evidence_claims.title: Long Shape Memory Alloy Tendon-based Soft Robotic Actuators and Implementation as a Soft Gripper
evidence_claims.claim: The modular soft gripper can be integrated as an end-effector on a commercial 6-DOF industrial robot arm (UR10) to execute pick-and-place tasks on real-world objects.

evidence_claims.title: A novel design of shape-memory alloy-based soft robotic gripper with variable stiffness
evidence_claims.claim: A single robotic finger achieves an approximate 18-fold stiffness variation between the liquid state (0.0136 N/mm) and solid state (0.2431 N/mm) of paraffin.

evidence_claims.title: A novel design of shape-memory alloy-based soft robotic gripper with variable stiffness
evidence_claims.claim: Variable stiffness joints enhance the gripper's maximum grasping force by approximately 10-fold, increasing from 0.57 N at low stiffness to 5.66 N at high stiffness.

evidence_claims.title: A novel design of shape-memory alloy-based soft robotic gripper with variable stiffness
evidence_claims.claim: Paraffin heating to its melting point of 58 °C with an embedded Ni-Cr wire takes about 70 s at 10 V, while natural cooling to the solid state takes about 380 s.

evidence_claims.title: A novel design of shape-memory alloy-based soft robotic gripper with variable stiffness
evidence_claims.claim: Independently modulating the stiffness of two embedded joints per finger combined with SMA wire actuation enables four distinct configurations: straight, joint-1 bending, joint-2 bending, and simultaneous bending.

evidence_claims.title: A novel design of shape-memory alloy-based soft robotic gripper with variable stiffness
evidence_claims.claim: At high stiffness, the soft gripper can stably hold a 500 g water bottle even after turning off power to the SMA actuator wire.

evidence_claims.title: A novel design of shape-memory alloy-based soft robotic gripper with variable stiffness
evidence_claims.claim: An analytical framework couples SMA Joule heating, empirical phase transformation kinetics, constitutive stress-strain relationships, and cantilever beam mechanics to relate heating time to joint bending angle.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Humanoid Hands with Large Grasping Force Enabled by Flexible Hybrid Pneumatic Actuators
evidence_claims.claim: A modular flexible hybrid pneumatic actuator incorporating an inner elastic bladder, rigid outer constraining rings, and a leaf spring backbone achieves high lateral/transverse stiffness while retaining axial bending flexibility.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Humanoid Hands with Large Grasping Force Enabled by Flexible Hybrid Pneumatic Actuators
evidence_claims.claim: An analytical mechanics model combining Euler-Bernoulli beam theory, volume conservation, and an empirical swelling correction predicts bending deformation with circular arc fitting errors below 0.86%.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Humanoid Hands with Large Grasping Force Enabled by Flexible Hybrid Pneumatic Actuators
evidence_claims.claim: An individual FHPA finger weighing approximately 50 g generates up to 15 N of output force and a 275-degree bending angle at 0.3 MPa air pressure, with an operating frequency exceeding 3 Hz.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Humanoid Hands with Large Grasping Force Enabled by Flexible Hybrid Pneumatic Actuators
evidence_claims.claim: Actuation output force scales with chamber count, reaching a maximum force of 42 N at 0.3 MPa for a four-chamber configuration.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Humanoid Hands with Large Grasping Force Enabled by Flexible Hybrid Pneumatic Actuators
evidence_claims.claim: Ring geometry directly influences bending mechanics: increasing torus ring thickness enhances bending angle, whereas increasing cylindrical ring thickness reduces bending angle.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Humanoid Hands with Large Grasping Force Enabled by Flexible Hybrid Pneumatic Actuators
evidence_claims.claim: Leaf spring material presents a tradeoff between force output and cyclic durability: 65Mn spring steel produces greater output force but suffers brittle fracture after 26,400 cycles, while SUS301 stainless steel survives 41,400 cycles before bladder rupture.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Humanoid Hands with Large Grasping Force Enabled by Flexible Hybrid Pneumatic Actuators
evidence_claims.claim: A 350 g five-DOF soft humanoid hand equipped with five FHPAs accomplishes both pinch and enveloping grasps on objects weighing between 3 g and 1366 g.

evidence_claims.title: Soft robotic fabric gripper with gecko adhesion and variable stiffness
evidence_claims.claim: A sheet-shaped fabric bending actuator fabricated using textile techniques (sewing and tube routing) enables edge/surface contact and planar integration of additional components, overcoming point-contact instability of fusiform actuators.

evidence_claims.title: Soft robotic fabric gripper with gecko adhesion and variable stiffness
evidence_claims.claim: Directional wedge-shaped gecko microstructures molded from Sylgard 170 on wax molds enhance surface holding force via van der Waals adhesion.

evidence_claims.title: Soft robotic fabric gripper with gecko adhesion and variable stiffness
evidence_claims.claim: A thermo-responsive variable stiffness filament (VSF) comprising a PET tube and internal heating coil achieves a ~26-fold bending stiffness variation (0.057 to 1.484 N/mm) between rigid and soft states.

evidence_claims.title: Soft robotic fabric gripper with gecko adhesion and variable stiffness
evidence_claims.claim: The tubular geometry of the VSF reduces thermal mass, enabling an ambient cooling time of 25 s alone and 31 s with gecko adhesive to transition from 80 °C to 50 °C.

evidence_claims.title: Soft robotic fabric gripper with gecko adhesion and variable stiffness
evidence_claims.claim: A simple analytical beam-bending model under quasi-hydrostatic and volume-invariance assumptions predicts finger bending angles up to 197.6° at 550 kPa.

evidence_claims.title: Soft robotic fabric gripper with gecko adhesion and variable stiffness
evidence_claims.claim: Integrating VSF and gecko adhesive increases peak holding force by up to 655% in the gripping mode and 507% in the pull-out mode for a 24 mm cylindrical object.

evidence_claims.title: Soft robotic fabric gripper with gecko adhesion and variable stiffness
evidence_claims.claim: The two-fingered gripper (3.7 g per finger) lifted payloads up to 1.1 kg, achieving a payload-to-weight ratio of 148.6 times.

evidence_claims.title: Soft robotic fabric gripper with gecko adhesion and variable stiffness
evidence_claims.claim: A stencil-printed conductive composite of EGaIn liquid metal and carbon grease provides bending strain feedback over 200 cycles with minimal drift (-1.79% expanding, -0.01% closing) without thermal interference from the VSF.

evidence_claims.title: Flexible self-powered multifunctional sensor for stiffness-tunable soft robotic gripper by multimaterial 3D printing

evidence_claims.claim: Field harvesting of mangosteens requires 7 seconds for unripe fruit (Level 1) and decreases to 4 seconds for ripe fruit (Level 4); the soft gripper is faster than human farmers for Level 2 (5 s vs. 7 s), but slower for Levels 3 and 4.

evidence_claims.title: Design of Telescopic Soft Gripper for Mangosteen Harvesting

evidence_claims.title: Soft Robotics for Chemists
evidence_claims.claim: Elastomeric pneumatic networks (PneuNets) with asymmetric wall compliance or composite layering produce continuous bending upon pressurization, where curvature scales inversely with material stiffness (e.g., Ecoflex achieves a radius of curvature of approximately 1.5 cm at 14 kPa compared to approximately 15 cm for PDMS).

evidence_claims.title: Soft Robotics for Chemists
evidence_claims.claim: Multilayer elastomeric actuators composed of two active Ecoflex PneuNet layers separated by a flat PDMS membrane can continuously alter their overall curvature from convex to concave depending on which network is pressurized.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Robotics for Chemists
evidence_claims.claim: Fully soft six-legged starfish-like grippers actuated through a single pressure inlet can passively conform to and lift delicate, irregularly shaped biological specimens (such as an uncooked chicken egg and an anesthetized mouse) without inflicting damage.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Robotics for Chemists
evidence_claims.claim: Patterning ridged topography into the elastomeric gripping surface introduces alternating gaps of air and elastomer, enhancing contact compliance and traction to sustain loads up to 300 g on smooth spheres up to 10 cm in diameter.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Robotics for Chemists
evidence_claims.claim: PneuNets actuated at 7 to 28 kPa require approximately 4 W per stroke and can sustain their deformed state passively for 10 minutes without substantial deflation when closed with a valve, before fully deflating over 60 minutes due to gas permeability and connection leakage.

evidence_claims.title: Soft robotic grippers: A review on technologies, materials, and applications
evidence_claims.claim: Fluidic elastomer actuators offer compliant deformation and simple fabrication, but external compressors/pumps restrict portability and fluidic channel impedance restricts response frequencies above 1 Hz.

evidence_claims.title: Soft robotic grippers: A review on technologies, materials, and applications
evidence_claims.claim: Granular and particle jamming mechanisms achieve rapid transition from compliant adaptation to rigid holding under vacuum, though conforming to deformable items after jamming remains problematic.

evidence_claims.title: Soft robotic grippers: A review on technologies, materials, and applications
evidence_claims.claim: Combining soft fluidic actuation with controllable adhesion or jamming enables decoupled shape and stiffness control, supporting payloads up to 100 to 1000 times the gripper self-weight.

evidence_claims.title: Soft robotic grippers: A review on technologies, materials, and applications
evidence_claims.claim: Dielectric elastomer actuators achieve actuation strains exceeding 100 percent with high energy density, but typically require high operating voltages and external rigid support frames to maintain stress output.

evidence_claims.title: Soft robotic grippers: A review on technologies, materials, and applications
evidence_claims.claim: Underactuation and virtually infinite degrees of freedom in soft continuum structures complicate modeling and control, prompting the use of reduced-order models and SOFA-based numerical simulation frameworks.

evidence_claims.title: Soft robotic grippers: A review on technologies, materials, and applications
evidence_claims.claim: Biodegradable gelatin biogels and elastomer formulations achieve ultimate strains over 300 percent and withstand more than 100,000 cycles, showing promise for sustainable or disposable soft robotic tools.

evidence_claims.title: Soft robotics gripper technology in medical surgery application: a systematic literature review
evidence_claims.claim: Soft robotic grippers fabricated from compliant materials (silicone, elastomers, hydrogels) conform to irregular tissue shapes and distribute pressure evenly, minimizing peak contact stresses and reducing the risk of tissue trauma during surgical manipulation compared to rigid instruments.

evidence_claims.title: Soft robotics gripper technology in medical surgery application: a systematic literature review
evidence_claims.claim: Soft morphing jaws can increase contact area by 20% to 30% over maximum allowable loads of rigid jaws and reduce contact pressure by approximately 30%, decreasing histological damage during simulated laparoscopic procedures.

evidence_claims.title: Soft robotics gripper technology in medical surgery application: a systematic literature review
evidence_claims.claim: Cyclic mechanical loading on Ecoflex silicone elastomer showed a Young's modulus decrease of approximately 20% between the first and second cycles due to polymer chain reorganization and microstructural fatigue.

evidence_claims.title: Soft robotics gripper technology in medical surgery application: a systematic literature review
evidence_claims.claim: Fatigue testing on silicone rubber cast soft pneumatic actuators demonstrated structural failure at an average of 3,439 inflation-deflation cycles under operational pressure, with observable micro-tears developing prior to rupture.

evidence_claims.title: Soft robotics gripper technology in medical surgery application: a systematic literature review
evidence_claims.claim: Variable-stiffness mechanisms (including granular jamming, layer jamming, and hybrid pneumatic locking actuators) permit real-time modulation between low compliance for safe tissue handling and higher rigidity for precise tasks such as suturing or retraction.

evidence_claims.title: Soft robotics gripper technology in medical surgery application: a systematic literature review
evidence_claims.claim: A clear functional division exists between continuum robot arms (which serve as hyper-redundant flexible robot bodies for anatomical navigation) and soft grippers (which serve as end-effectors for safe grasping and atraumatic tissue manipulation).

evidence_claims.title: Soft robotics gripper technology in medical surgery application: a systematic literature review
evidence_claims.claim: Topology optimization and Finite Element Analysis (FEA) enable optimized material distribution and prediction of stress, deformation, and response time in soft robotic grippers prior to fabrication.

evidence_claims.title: Soft robotics gripper technology in medical surgery application: a systematic literature review
evidence_claims.claim: Supervised autonomous algorithms and reinforcement learning in soft tissue robotic systems (such as the STAR platform) enable autonomous suturing and anastomosis with greater consistency and fewer mistakes compared to manual execution.

evidence_claims.title: Soft robotics gripper technology in medical surgery application: a systematic literature review
evidence_claims.claim: Soft robotic grippers manufactured via 3D printing or casting can be produced at low unit costs (under $200 to $500, or actuator costs under $1,000) compared to traditional rigid robotic systems that cost approximately $20,000.

evidence_claims.title: TRIGGER: A Lightweight Universal Jamming Gripper for Aerial Grasping
evidence_claims.claim: A universal jamming gripper can attain its maximum holding force with a substantially reduced activation force (250 gf / 2.5 N) by utilizing lower granular fill ratios (66% compared to 90%).

evidence_claims.title: TRIGGER: A Lightweight Universal Jamming Gripper for Aerial Grasping
evidence_claims.claim: Mixing a deadener additive (up to 15% by weight) into the silicone membrane enhances maximum holding force by up to 52% (from 10.1 N to 15.4 N) through increased membrane softness, conformability, and surface friction.

evidence_claims.title: TRIGGER: A Lightweight Universal Jamming Gripper for Aerial Grasping
evidence_claims.claim: The uniaxial contact behavior of a transitioning universal jamming gripper can be modeled as two parallel non-linear compression springs representing the air-filled membrane and the jammed structure using power-law force-displacement relations.

evidence_claims.title: TRIGGER: A Lightweight Universal Jamming Gripper for Aerial Grasping
evidence_claims.claim: A universal jamming gripper attached to a multicopter in a claw configuration can perform dual duty as landing gear, providing passive compliance to absorb landing shocks and eliminating the need for dedicated landing gear.

evidence_claims.title: TRIGGER: A Lightweight Universal Jamming Gripper for Aerial Grasping
evidence_claims.claim: Aerial grasping success with a soft jamming gripper is strongly shape-dependent, excelling on geometries with vertical faces (cube, ridge) but suffering from slippage on spherical surfaces and complete failure on wedging geometries (pyramid).

evidence_claims.title: Universal Jamming Gripper: Experimental Analysis on Envelope and Granular Materials
evidence_claims.claim: Universal jamming grippers function through two distinct operational states: a relaxed atmospheric state allowing passive geometric adaptation to objects, and an evacuated jammed state where granular particle compaction induces petrification and stiffness increase to retain grasped objects.

evidence_claims.title: Universal Jamming Gripper: Experimental Analysis on Envelope and Granular Materials
evidence_claims.claim: Grasp engagement and retention in universal jamming grippers depend on three distinct physical mechanisms: static friction forces at microscopic contact interfaces, geometric constraints providing normal retention forces, and vacuum chambers creating suction pressure differentials.

evidence_claims.title: Universal Jamming Gripper: Experimental Analysis on Envelope and Granular Materials
evidence_claims.claim: Membrane wall thickness strongly modulates grasp friction: a thin latex envelope (0.15 mm) transmits internal granular morphology to the external surface to create macroscopic waviness (reaching 74.86 µm for 1.0 mm beads), whereas thicker silicone walls (1.0–2.0 mm) cushion and conceal internal particle relief.

evidence_claims.title: Universal Jamming Gripper: Experimental Analysis on Envelope and Granular Materials
evidence_claims.claim: Energy absorbed during pull-off serves as an index of grasp robustness against dynamic inertial forces and vibrations, scaling inversely with envelope Shore hardness among silicones and achieving peak values exceeding 10 mJ in thin latex combined with 0.3–0.4 mm glass beads.

evidence_claims.title: Universal Jamming Gripper: Experimental Analysis on Envelope and Granular Materials
evidence_claims.claim: The deformation force required during passive compression is primarily governed by envelope membrane elasticity and thickness rather than grain size alone, with Shore 00-10 silicone exhibiting near-zero deformation force while Shore A-25 exceeded 20 N.

evidence_claims.title: Comparison of interfacing mechanics for soft robotic grippers
evidence_claims.claim: Equipping bare PLA arms of an underactuated tarsal-chain-inspired soft gripper with dedicated interfacing structures significantly improves grasping and transport success across diverse everyday objects.

evidence_claims.title: Comparison of interfacing mechanics for soft robotic grippers
evidence_claims.claim: High-friction polymer interfaces dramatically outperform compliant bubble pads and hairy brush strips across almost all arbitrary macroscopic objects, demonstrating that surface friction dominates compliance in universal macroscopic gripping.

evidence_claims.title: Comparison of interfacing mechanics for soft robotic grippers
evidence_claims.claim: Hairy brush interfaces rely primarily on mechanical interlocking with substrate asperities or open grid geometries rather than surface friction, failing completely on smooth surfaces such as ceramic vases and bicycle helmets.

evidence_claims.title: Comparison of interfacing mechanics for soft robotic grippers
evidence_claims.claim: The effective Young's moduli of insect-inspired gripper interface modules range from 1.58e-4 to 12.65e-4 GPa, matching the softness regime of organic cartilage and allowing passive compliance to surface features under compressive gripping loads.

evidence_claims.title: Comparison of interfacing mechanics for soft robotic grippers
evidence_claims.claim: Applying a friction-enhancing rubber spray to highly compliant bubble pads increases grasping success from 0-80% to 33-100%, indicating that structural compliance requires sufficient interface friction to achieve stable grasping.

evidence_claims.title: Comparison of interfacing mechanics for soft robotic grippers
evidence_claims.claim: Direct geometric scaling of biological hairy attachment structures to macroscopic human-scale grippers without contact splitting, stiffness gradients, or specialized tip geometries severely degrades attachment effectiveness due to unfavorable area-to-mass scaling.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Manipulators and Grippers: A Review
evidence_claims.claim: Soft manipulator design operates within a 2D qualitative design space characterized by trade-offs between precision and degrees of freedom, and between structural compliance and force exertion.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Manipulators and Grippers: A Review
evidence_claims.claim: 3D printing enables the fabrication of complex, amorphous geometries and embedded microfluidic channels or logic, but printable soft materials are relatively brittle compared to molded elastomers and less suited for high-pressure actuation.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Manipulators and Grippers: A Review
evidence_claims.claim: Modeling continuum soft manipulators requires methods beyond rigid-body kinematics, including constant curvature approximations, Jacobian methods, feed-forward neural networks, real-time finite element modeling (FEM), and discrete voxel mass-spring lattice simulators.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Manipulators and Grippers: A Review
evidence_claims.claim: Variable stiffness can be implemented in soft manipulators via particle jamming (locking granular media under vacuum) or through adjustable stiffness layers integrated into pneumatic actuators.
evidence_claims.evidence_type: literature review of variable stiffness mechanisms

evidence_claims.title: Soft Manipulators and Grippers: A Review
evidence_claims.claim: Passive underactuated soft grippers made of compliant materials such as hot melt adhesive can achieve force and form closure purely through structural deformation and contact interaction forces without active motors.

evidence_claims.title: Soft Manipulators and Grippers: A Review
evidence_claims.claim: Soft sensing faces substantial challenges because infinite degrees of freedom preclude one-to-one sensor-to-DOF mapping, wiring connections risk impeding robot compliance, and ionic resistive sensors struggle to isolate strain from pressure without multi-layered architectures.

evidence_claims.title: Design of a Granular Jamming Universal Gripper
evidence_claims.claim: A universal gripper can be fabricated at low cost (less than $20) using a latex balloon filled with granular material attached to a 4 cm radius funnel with a cloth filter.

evidence_claims.title: Design of a Granular Jamming Universal Gripper
evidence_claims.claim: Optimization of filling volume to 50% and funnel radius to 4 cm enables complete membrane deflation and firm granular interlocking around objects, whereas over-filling (75%) or smaller funnels (3.5 cm) constrain granule mobility.

evidence_claims.title: Design of a Granular Jamming Universal Gripper
evidence_claims.claim: Actuation via a 220 V electric vacuum pump achieved a 100% grasping success rate (5/5 trials) across 8 daily-life objects of varying shapes, sizes, and stiffness.

evidence_claims.title: Design of a Granular Jamming Universal Gripper
evidence_claims.claim: A 60 ml medical syringe can act as a manual vacuum actuator, achieving membrane conformation in under 2 seconds with grasping success rates between 60% and 100% across tested objects.

evidence_claims.title: Design of a Granular Jamming Universal Gripper
evidence_claims.claim: Fine gram flour powder provides superior interlocking capability and grasping performance compared to coarse ground coffee powder due to finer particle geometry.

evidence_claims.title: Design of a Granular Jamming Universal Gripper
evidence_claims.claim: Grasping force fluctuates with the volume of granular filling and the volume of evacuated air inside the flexible membrane.

limitations.text: Actuator range of motion reaches an upper limit around a volume ratio of 1.8 where force chains cause particles to behave as a rigid solid, resisting further bending and risking membrane rupture near the inlet
Bending angle of the prototype actuator is relatively small (around 90°), requiring an additional mechanism to grasp large objects
The actuator cannot fully restore to its unactuated baseline without active external vibration due to particle jamming and limited silicone restoring force
Introduced vibration may be undesirable in certain operating environments
Optimal power and frequency for the embedded vibrators were not determined
High stiffness increase may be unsuitable for delicate objects requiring gentle contact, such as eggs
Actuation output force is significantly lower than input piston force because much of the input work is redirected into particle jamming
Motion accuracy and repeatability degrade as injected volume increases (standard deviation increases up to 3° at V = 1.8)
Analytical model treats deformation as an idealized uniform torus and ignores localized bulging, cylinder wall friction, and dynamic granular packing effects
Integrating rigid electric drive cylinders and vibration motors introduces rigid elements, mass, and wiring that compromise the total compliance and compactness of the soft robotic system
Long-term durability, cyclic fatigue of the silicone membrane, particle wear, and actuation speed/bandwidth were not evaluated
Heating time from ambient room temperature (20 °C) to 45 °C is approximately 40 s, which is too long for practical applications without preheating.
Ventilation feature dimensions cannot exceed critical bounds without risking physical separation of conductive TPU from the substrate during bending.
Theoretical resistance modeling diverges substantially from experimental measurements at bending angles greater than 90 degrees due to unmodeled material effects.
Joint bending angles must be restricted to a maximum of 90 degrees in practice to maintain estimation accuracy.
Joint temperature was controlled within a band (45–50 °C) rather than a precise setpoint, introducing thermal drift and measurement variability in resistance.
Embedding thermocouples for closed-loop thermal control without altering finger compliance and stiffness remains an unresolved challenge.
Long-term position feedback repeatability and operational cycle life of SMP and conductive TPU have not yet been evaluated across extended cycles.
Simplifications in theoretical stiffness modeling (cantilever beam approximation and neglecting fiber reinforcement) caused quantitative discrepancies with experimental force measurements.
The analytical stiffness model is restricted to zero pneumatic pressure and does not capture stiffening behavior under combined pneumatic pressurization and thermal state changes.
Thermal transition times (10 s heating with preheating, 15 s cooling) limit dynamic response rates and real-time stiffness modulation bandwidth.
Position feedback validation was performed quasi-statically at discrete pressure steps without evaluating dynamic grasping, external payload disturbances, or obstacle contacts.
Inherent piezoresistive elastomer drift and thermal cross-sensitivity may degrade calibration stability over prolonged operation without frequent baseline calibration.
Long operational transition time required for returning from the low-stiffness state to the high-stiffness state due to slow passive heat dissipation of the heated SMP
Inherent softness and small actuation force generated by soft SMA actuators (approx. 10^-3 to 10^-1 N) when unreinforced

Minor discrepancies between theoretical and experimental bending modulus values (mean errors of 5.6% in high stiffness and 1.7% in low stiffness) caused by SMP fabrication tolerances and positioning errors during embedding
Passive cooling duration of 240 seconds makes the gripper unsuitable for high-speed dynamic or industrial pick-and-place manipulation tasks without active cooling
Actuated SMA wires must be continuously energized during the 240-second cooling period to maintain shape until SMP solidifies, increasing overall energy consumption
Low glass transition temperature of SMP (55 °C) restricts operation in elevated thermal environments where stiffness modulation would fail
Maximum grasping force (5.8 N) remains modest compared to rigid or fluidic high-pressure grippers, limiting applications to light or delicate objects
Absence of integrated embedded curvature or contact force feedback sensors requires open-loop timing-based control

The joint torque model assumes strain is localized to the thin membrane, full membrane contact occurs, and joint angle effects on moment arm are negligible, causing model inaccuracies including overprediction at low pressures/higher joint angles and underprediction at high pressures due to membrane bulging.
Adhesion is temporarily degraded by dust, dirt, or porous surfaces (though cleanable using a tacky surface).
Because elastomer actuators possess low inherent bending stiffness, adhesive performance on flat surfaces is poor without active shear preloads or actuation-independent stiffening mechanisms.
Directional wedge adhesives require a shear load to engage, precluding normal-only engagement without active or geometric shear generation.
The torque model serves primarily as a design tool for geometry rather than for real-time state estimation and control.
Manufacturing chambers with 0.9 mm membrane walls and 2 mm chamber widths approached the practical limits of the casting process.
Testing was restricted to smooth polycarbonate cylinders and a small number of rigid household items, leaving performance on compliant, rough, or delicate textured surfaces uncharacterized.
Long-term interfacial fatigue and delamination risks between the DragonSkin and MoldStar silicone layers under repeated shear loading were not evaluated beyond 25 manipulation cycles.
Disengagement dynamics, release speed, and passive release reliability under transient or perturbing shear loads were not systematically measured.
Manual manufacturing steps involving polycarbonate shims and spin-coating may result in fabrication variability between individual actuator fingers.
The empirical finger stiffness was lower than theoretical predictions due to compliance in the mechanical connections between the finger and the gripper body.
The dynamic contact force magnitude was constrained by the physical limits of the prototype components.
The open-loop control scheme requires desired gripping forces, object sizes, and crush thresholds to be predefined or premeasured experimentally before execution.
Grasping capacity is subject to the payload, size, and motor torque limits of the physical prototype.
Open-loop operation requires prior knowledge of object dimensions and crush thresholds; unexpected variations or slip cannot be sensed or corrected on-the-fly.
Close mechanical tolerances between the rotating inner shaft and the outer frame are critical; excessive clearance or wear could introduce backlash or degrade stiffness predictability.
A 90-degree rotation time of ~0.8 s may constrain applications requiring millisecond-scale on-the-fly stiffness switching during high-speed cycle times.
Orthogonal arrangement of two flexure sections limits variable compliance primarily to the 2D plane (XY), offering limited compliance to out-of-plane torsional or axial shock loads.
The Cosserat-based grasping force formulation is highly nonlinear and lacks an analytical closed-form solution, requiring iterative shooting numerical computations

Model predictive errors increase markedly when bending torque exceeds 40 Nmm or deflection offset Z exceeds 55 mm because large deformations near the critical bending torque cause complex nonlinear responses that cannot be easily modeled
Direct closed-loop feedback control of pulling force using a sensor is difficult because the SMA-1 wire is wrapped tightly around pulleys inside a cavity too small to accommodate a force sensor
Electrothermal contraction of SMA-1 exhibits an inherently nonlinear response that complicates controller design
Friction coefficients at the fingertip degrade over repeated grasping trials due to surface wear on the 3D-printed PLA, leading to modeling mismatches if static friction values are assumed
The modeling and experimental evaluations are restricted to two-dimensional planar bending in the XOZ plane, leaving 3D out-of-plane torsional or lateral deflections unmodeled
Objects are restricted to rigid flat cuboids; compliance, curvature, and geometric irregularities of grasped objects are not represented in the formulation
Thermal dynamics, heat dissipation rates, cooling transition latencies, and hysteretic behavior during cycling of the SMA wires were not incorporated into the static model
Closed-loop real-time force feedback control was not demonstrated on the physical prototype, relying instead on static position-based (Z offset) estimation and open-loop thermal actuation
Miniaturization of fluidic elastomer and externally motorized grippers is constrained by heavy and bulky external pumps, compressors, and motor assemblies
FEA actuation frequencies above 1 Hz are difficult to achieve due to fluidic channel impedance and required flow rates
DEAs produce low active output stress, necessitating multilayer stacking that complicates device fabrication
High operational voltages (several kilovolts) in DEAs and electroadhesion introduce risk of external electrical discharges
IPMC actuators exhibit slow operating response, low output stress, poor thermodynamic efficiency, and actuation hysteresis
Thermal variable-stiffness materials (LMPAs, SMPs, SMAs) suffer from slow solidifying and cooling response times dominated by thermal conduction and convective dissipation
SMAs exhibit cyclic actuation hysteresis, require high electric driving currents, and possess low thermodynamic efficiency
Granular jamming grippers cannot grasp flat objects due to inability to envelope/cage them, and cannot adjust to shape changes of deformable objects once solidified
ER and MR fluids provide relatively low absolute structural stiffness due to limited yield stress (up to 250 kPa)
Electroadhesion and geckoadhesion require clean and relatively dry target surfaces, and electroadhesion exhibits residual charge hysteresis upon voltage removal
Geckoadhesion struggles to adhere to rough surfaces and low surface-energy materials, and highly compliant substrates may hinder target release
Suction mechanisms require smooth, nonporous object surfaces to maintain vacuum seals
Elastomeric components often suffer from a lack of long-term mechanical robustness
Resistive strain sensors display history-dependent resistance (hysteresis) that complicates calibration, whereas capacitive sensors require more complex readout circuitry
Performance metrics compiled across heterogeneous published studies reflect differing experimental methodologies and setups rather than standardized benchmarking protocols

Combining multiple functional modalities (e.g., actuation plus variable stiffness and sensing) substantially increases manufacturing complexity and failure modes

Experiments were conducted in open-loop without closed-loop feedback control of temperature, stiffness, or bending angles
Achieving the passive shape-locked state requires actively pressurizing the actuator and activating Joule heating before cooling and depressurizing
Object grasping demonstrations served only as a proof of concept without optimizing joint activation for different objects
Thermal fatigue, cyclic life, and interface delamination between the silicone matrix and CPLA over extensive thermal-pneumatic cycling were not characterized
Hysteresis between resistivity and temperature was neglected in favor of a linear approximation, which may introduce model inaccuracy during dynamic transient heating

Continuous power is required during the shape modulation and transition phase, which may impact energy efficiency during rapid dynamic tasks

Friction between the sliding rod and holding pins was neglected in the dynamic model formulation for simplicity.
The stiffness of unknown grasped objects cannot be calculated in advance, making precise model-based grasp modeling inherently inaccurate and necessitating robust control.
System feedback relies on an inexpensive (£9) 1D Force Sensing Resistor (FSR) with variable resistance rather than a precision multi-axis load cell.

The assumption of an inelastic tendon may degrade over extensive cyclic operation due to tendon creep or elasticity, affecting stiffness calibration and force precision.

High pulling forces rely heavily on friction; reducing surface friction drastically reduces pulling capacity

The systematic literature review is restricted to 24 included studies matching narrow search keywords within Scopus-indexed journals (2015-2024), which may overlook relevant developments in conference proceedings, non-indexed literature, or other databases

The 1 to 5 optimization scoring assigned to machine learning algorithms appears to be a heuristic/qualitative assessment synthesized by the review authors rather than a pooled statistical meta-analysis across standardized benchmark tasks

Several reported clinical benefits (such as exact wound healing times, pain scores, and reoperation rates in summary tables) represent projected or preliminary claims from selected trials/simulations rather than outcomes established across large-scale randomized human clinical trials

Miniature low-power pumps result in longer cycle times (11 s vs 4 s in high-power setups) and a lower vacuum pressure differential (approx. 28 kPa vs >80 kPa in stationary systems).
The bag-shaped membrane generates horizontal reaction forces that cause slippage on rounded or slanted shapes (such as spheres and tubes).
Grasping fails on wedging geometries (pyramids) and shapes with insufficient contact surface area (triangles).

The multi-second evacuation cycle time leaves the hovering aerial platform vulnerable to external wind disturbances and ground effect drift while waiting for particle jamming to complete.
Relying primarily on friction and surface adhesion without geometric interlocking makes holding performance sensitive to surface contamination, dust accumulation, and moisture.

The gripper remains purely passive with a single non-discretized actuation chamber.
The prototypes lack integrated tactile sensors, real-time sensing feedback, and closed-loop grasping control.
Testing was conducted exclusively against a single standardized PA12 mushroom-shaped specimen.

Testing was restricted entirely to quasi-static, purely vertical traction (20 mm/min) against a single rigid geometry, without evaluating off-axis, shear, torsional, or high-speed dynamic manipulations.

The study is exploratory in nature, establishing qualitative guidelines rather than definitive conclusions for specific use-cases.
Actuation was executed manually via a handle pulled by a human operator without direct measurement of the applied input actuation force.

Scaling constraints (surface area scaling with length squared while mass scales with length cubed) impede the effectiveness of macroscopic hair arrays without contact splitting.
Original bubble and brush materials had very low baseline surface friction, necessitating post-hoc rubber spray treatment to decouple compliance from friction.
Manual actuation by a human operator introduces operator-dependent variability in pulling velocity, peak tendon force, and arm closing trajectories.
Static friction characterization was conducted exclusively on flat, rigid substrates, which may not capture friction dynamics on curved, compliant, or irregular geometries.
Dynamic friction, wear endurance, shear fatigue, and adhesive degradation over extended cyclic grasping were not assessed.
Testing only two arbitrary orientations per object may not encompass edge-case grasping poses encountered in automated manipulation.
The use of repurposed packaging foam and Velcro introduces uncontrolled compliance, damping, and potential interfacial hysteresis between the gripper structure and the contact pad.
Soft manipulators inherently suffer from lower grasping force, lower precision, and a lack of repeatability compared to rigid robots.
High or infinite degrees of freedom make precise kinematic control and modeling challenging and computationally intensive.
Soft materials present challenges regarding non-linear responses, difficulty in simulation and modeling, requirements for self-repair, fatigue failure, and fabrication limits.
Layered casting and soft lithography methods tend to constrain robot morphology to planar shapes rather than fully amorphous 3D geometries.
3D-printed flexible materials remain relatively brittle compared to molded silicone rubbers, restricting their utility in pressurized actuation.
Cable-driven actuation requires external rotary or linear actuation sources, which can make systems bulky.

Soft sensing lacks one-to-one pairing of sensor to degree of freedom; ionic sensors cannot decouple strain and pressure without specialized multi-layer designs; flexible electronics withstand only minimal strain; and optical tactile sensors require rigid cameras positioned close to the deformation zone.
Physical connections (electrodes, wires) to soft sensors can restrict the compliance and dynamic behavior of soft robotic systems.
Scientific progress in understanding and fabricating soft manipulators trails behind the demands and aspirations of practical applications.
As a qualitative review paper, no primary empirical bench tests or quantitative comparative datasets were generated across the surveyed mechanisms.
The proposed four-axis design space trade-offs are presented qualitatively without formal mathematical models or validated bounds.

Long-term fatigue, cyclic creep, thermal dissipation (specifically for shape memory alloys), and environmental degradation of soft polymers are discussed conceptually rather than comprehensively quantified.
Testing is preliminary and limited to a controlled laboratory environment rather than industrial pick-and-place scenarios.
Initial vacuum pump tests failed to jam granules until fabric porosity and filling volume constraints were adjusted.
Current system connects directly to the vacuum source without pressure regulation to modulate negative pressure against grasping performance.
Grasping performance drops significantly (down to 40%) for small objects (e.g., bottle cap, glue stick) when using weaker actuation methods.
The prototype lacks sensory feedback (e.g., internal pressure or tactile sensing).
Detailed stiffness analysis, force characterization, and finite element modeling (FEM) were not performed in this study.
Testing was conducted using manual handling rather than full autonomous robotic arm deployment.
Grasping evaluation relied on a small sample size (5 trials per condition) with binary pass/fail criteria (held for 5 s) rather than continuous force, payload, or slip measurements.
All 120 grasping trials were executed via manual operator handling and positioning of the gripper, meaning automated robotic positioning errors and dynamic arm accelerations were not evaluated.
Membrane wear, puncture susceptibility against sharp objects, and fatigue life under cyclic jamming were not investigated.
Manual lung deflation via a straw is impractical and unhygienic for real-world assistive applications, and data for it was only reported for 2 of the 8 objects.
No mathematical or numerical constitutive continuum/discrete models were developed to describe the mechanics of jamming and contact.

gap_implications.text: Demonstrates that dry granular materials can act simultaneously as an actuation transmission medium and a variable stiffness mechanism, bypassing the need for fluid seals and pneumatic pumps; however, this single study does not prove general suitability across all soft robotics due to motion range saturation and the necessity of auxiliary vibrators for restoration.
A 10–15 s thermal response time may prevent applications requiring rapid, adaptive stiffness switching during dynamic grasping tasks.
Limiting joint bending to 90° to avoid resistance modeling errors restricts the kinematic grasping envelope of the finger.
Lack of closed-loop temperature control and potential sensor drift may hinder precise position and force regulation in uncalibrated or changing ambient thermal conditions.
Absence of a combined electromechanical-pneumatic model limits model-based control of variable-stiffness soft actuators under simultaneous inflation and thermal modulation.

Demonstrates that thermally induced phase change can resolve the force-density drawback of soft SMA grippers, but highlights slow thermal dissipation as a critical barrier, motivating research into active cooling or non-thermal variable-stiffness mechanisms

Suggests that multi-joint soft digits capable of multi-posture pre-shaping and area contact provide substantial grasping advantages over monolithic single-curvature soft fingers for complex geometries
